# kayjs-mail

> Mail for kay apps: SMTP configured from typed environment variables, mails written as `.kay` components rendered to html and text, an outbox in development and tests instead of a real server, and sending through kay's queue with retries. It works from kay pages, actions and jobs, and from a plain Elysia app.

## Rules that are easy to get wrong

- Mail clients drop stylesheets: a mail's styles live in `style` attributes. The components kayjs-mail ships already do, themed through kay's library settings; Tailwind classes do nothing in a mail.
- `from` is the site's own address, whose domain the SMTP server signs for: a visitor's address goes in `replyTo`, never in `from`, or SPF and DKIM fail and the mail lands in spam.
- In development (`NODE_ENV=development`) and under `bun test` (`NODE_ENV=test`) no mail leaves the process: they go to the outbox, which the development server lists at `/_kay/mail` and a test reads through `outbox`. Only another `NODE_ENV`, production, sends over SMTP.
- `send()` throws when the server refuses the mail or cannot be reached. An action whose point is not the mail itself uses `enqueue()`, so a mail server outage never fails the visitor's action, and the queue retries it.
- `enqueue()` renders the mail at once and queues the result: the queue runs only in a server that uses the mailer, listed in `kay.config.ts` with `mailExtension` or used as `new Elysia().use(mail)`.

## Setup

kayjs-mail is published as `@kaynooo/kayjs-mail` to `https://git.kaynooo.fr/api/packages/kaynooo/npm/`, beside kay. kay and Elysia are peer dependencies.

```ts
// src/mail.ts
import { mailer } from '@kaynooo/kayjs-mail'

export const mail = mailer({ from: 'Site <contact@example.com>', lang: 'fr' })
```

```ts
// kay.config.ts
import { mailExtension } from '@kaynooo/kayjs-mail'
import { defineConfig } from 'kay/server'

export default defineConfig({ extensions: [mailExtension(async () => (await import('./src/mail')).mail)] })
```

- `mailExtension(load)` hands the mailer to `pages()`, which uses it before the pages: `src/server.ts` needs no `.use(mail)`. `load` imports the module only as `pages()` builds the app, never as `kay check`, the editor or `kay build` read the config: a `.kay` mail imported while the config loads comes before kay compiles any, so `kay.config.ts` never imports `src/mail.ts` itself.
- An Elysia app not served by `pages()` uses it as a plugin instead: `new Elysia().use(mail)`.

- `mailer(options)` returns an Elysia plugin: the server using it, through `mailExtension` or `.use(mail)`, runs the queue `enqueue` fills and, in development, serves the outbox page. A script that only sends need not use it.
- Options: `from`, the default sender, `SMTP_FROM` when left out; `fromName`, the name shown beside a bare `SMTP_FROM`; `to`, the recipient of a mail naming none, `MAIL_TO` when left out, read from the environment in development too; `lang`, the `<html lang>` of the mail documents, `en` by default, which a message's own `lang` replaces; `transport`, where mails go in place of the default; `queue`, kay's `QueueOptions` (`attempts`, `backoff`, `store`, `onFailed`...) plus `name`, `mail` by default, which two mailers in one app set apart; `optional`, see Environment.

## Environment

In production the mailer reads, as the server boots, through kay's `defineEnv`:

| Variable | |
| --- | --- |
| `SMTP_HOST` | required |
| `SMTP_PORT` | `465` by default: TLS from the start; another port upgrades with STARTTLS |
| `SMTP_USER`, `SMTP_PASS` | both or neither, for a server needing no login; with a password and a port other than 465, a server not offering STARTTLS is refused |
| `SMTP_RATE_LIMIT` | optional: the most mails a second, for a provider capping the rate |
| `SMTP_DKIM_SELECTOR`, `SMTP_DKIM_PRIVATE_KEY` | both or neither: signs each mail with DKIM, for a relay that does not, the public key published at `<selector>._domainkey.<domain>`; the PEM key's line breaks may be written `\n` to hold it on one line |
| `SMTP_DKIM_DOMAIN` | the domain the signature vouches for, the sender's by default |
| `SMTP_FROM` | required unless `mailer({ from })` gives the sender: `Name <address>` or a bare address |
| `MAIL_TO` | optional: where a mail naming no `to` goes, such as a contact form's, unless `mailer({ to })` gives it; addresses apart by commas, a name holding none |

A missing or refused variable stops the boot, naming each one. `kay build` runs without them and leaves them to the server. The client greets the server with the sender's domain, not the container's hostname, and gives up on a server silent for 10 seconds. It keeps up to 5 connections open while mails keep coming, so a burst reuses them, and closes them a second after the last mail, so a script ends. Development and tests need none of them.

`mailer({ optional: true })` boots without `SMTP_HOST` and `SMTP_FROM` instead, for a site whose mail can wait to be set up: `mail.configured` reads `false`, and `send` and `enqueue` throw `MailNotConfigured`, whose `missing` names the variables, before rendering or queueing anything, so a contact form can catch it and tell the visitor to write or call instead. A mail naming no `to` while the mailer has none, in any environment, throws it naming `MAIL_TO`, alongside the others, so a contact form sends to `MAIL_TO` with nothing to check itself. An app throws it too for a setting of its own, `new MailNotConfigured(['SUPPORT_PHONE'])`.

## Writing a mail

A mail is a `.kay` component like any other, rendered on the server with `renderToString` from `kay/server`, its `await` blocks waited for. kayjs-mail ships the pieces most mails need, each with inline styles:

```kay
---
import Button from '@kaynooo/kayjs-mail/button.kay'
import Heading from '@kaynooo/kayjs-mail/heading.kay'
import Layout from '@kaynooo/kayjs-mail/layout.kay'
import Paragraph from '@kaynooo/kayjs-mail/paragraph.kay'

const { name, url } = props<{ name: string, url: string }>()
---
Layout(preheader="Your account is ready")
  @footer
    | Sent by Example
  Heading Welcome, {name}
  Paragraph Confirm your address to start.
  Button(href={url}) Confirm my address
  Paragraph(muted) Or paste #[a(href={url}) {url}] into your browser.
```

- `Layout` fills the window with the background colour and centres a card; `preheader` is the line clients show beside the subject, hidden in the mail itself; `@footer` sits under the card.
- They hold in Outlook for Windows, which renders mails with Word: the card keeps its width through a table only Outlook reads, and the button stays padded and clickable as a whole. The document carries the head Outlook needs to keep its scale.
- `Heading` (`level` 1, 2 or 3, 1 by default), `Paragraph` (`muted` for the small print), `Button(href)` and `Link(href)` take their text as children; `Link` sits inside a paragraph: `Paragraph Read #[Link(href={url}) the guide].`
- `Code` shows a one-time or verification code, large, spaced and in `mono`, selected whole by one click where the client allows it: `Code {code}`.
- `Divider` is a line across the card.
- `Image(src alt width height)` takes its width in pixels, which Outlook sizes it by; other clients scale it down to a narrow screen. `height` is optional.
- `Row` lays `Column`s side by side, stacking them on a screen too narrow for them: `Column` takes half the card's width, or `share`, the fraction it takes, `Column(share={1 / 3})`.
- `Fields(fields)` lays out a form's answers as label and value pairs, `fields` a list of `{ label, value?, href? }` (the `Field` type): a long value wraps, its line breaks kept, `href` links it, a `mailto:` or `tel:` say, and a value blank or left out shows `empty`, `-` by default. The text part writes each as `Label: value`, one to a line.
- `Quote(text)` sets a block of text a visitor wrote apart, its line breaks kept in the html and the text part alike.
- Their colours, fonts, radius and width come from the library's settings, which the app replaces in `kay.config.ts` as with any kay library: `settings: { '@kaynooo/kayjs-mail': './src/mail-settings.ts' }`, a module default-exporting `{ ...defaults, accent: '#0047ff' }`, `defaults` and the `Settings` type imported from `@kaynooo/kayjs-mail`.
- In a client's dark mode, Apple Mail and Outlook.com among them, `Layout` and the components switch to dark colours: `settings.dark` gives any of `text`, `muted`, `background`, `surface`, `border`, `accent` and `onAccent`, and each left out is derived from its light colour, lightness turned over and the accent lightened until it reads on the card; only hex colours are derived, another is kept as it is. `darkPalette(settings)` gives the colours a mail would switch to. The rules sit in a `<style>` the document moves into its head, beside `color-scheme` metas saying `light dark`; a mail without them declares `light` alone, so no client inverts part of it. The Gmail apps apply their own dark mode whatever the mail says.
- A component's markup is wrapped in a whole html document, with the charset, the viewport and the subject as its title; markup that already starts with `<html>` or a doctype is kept as it is.

A contact form's mail, the visitor's answers listed and their message quoted:

```kay
---
import Button from '@kaynooo/kayjs-mail/button.kay'
import Fields from '@kaynooo/kayjs-mail/fields.kay'
import Heading from '@kaynooo/kayjs-mail/heading.kay'
import Layout from '@kaynooo/kayjs-mail/layout.kay'
import Quote from '@kaynooo/kayjs-mail/quote.kay'

const { name, email, phone, topic, message } = props<{ name: string, email: string, phone?: string, topic: string, message: string }>()

const fields = [
  { label: 'Name', value: name },
  { label: 'Email', value: email, href: `mailto:${email}` },
  { label: 'Phone', value: phone, href: phone && `tel:${phone.replaceAll(' ', '')}` },
]
---
Layout(preheader={message.slice(0, 120)})
  @footer
    | Sent from the contact form. Replying to this mail writes to {name}.
  Heading {topic}
  Fields(fields={fields} empty="not given")
  Quote(text={message})
  Button(href={`mailto:${email}?subject=${encodeURIComponent(`Re: ${topic}`)}`}) Reply to {name}
```

It goes out with `replyTo: { name, address: email }`, so replying reaches the visitor, and `from` stays the site's own.

## Sending

```kay
--- server
import { s } from 'kay'
import { mail } from '../mail'
import Welcome from '../mails/welcome.kay'

export const signUp = action(s.Object({ name: s.String({ maxLength: 100 }), email: s.String({ format: 'email', maxLength: 254 }) }), async ({ name, email }) => {
  await mail.enqueue({ to: email, subject: `Welcome, ${name}`, view: Welcome, props: { name, url: 'https://example.com/confirm' } })
})
---
```

- A message takes `to` (the mailer's `to` or `MAIL_TO` when left out), `cc` and `bcc` (an address or a list), `replyTo`, `from`, `subject`, `lang`, `headers`, `attachments` (`{ filename, content, contentType?, cid? }`, `content` a string or bytes) and `unsubscribe`, and its content: `view` and `props` for a component (`props` left out when it takes none required), `html` for markup made elsewhere, or `text` alone.
- A message's `lang` is its `<html lang>` and the locale its component renders in, so `t()` and the formatters from `kay/i18n` read the recipient's language: one of the site's locales, `renderToString` refusing another. Without it the component renders in the site's default locale, or the request's while one runs.
- `unsubscribe` offers one-click unsubscribe (RFC 8058), which Gmail and Yahoo require of bulk senders: an https URL that unsubscribes the recipient when it receives a POST, or `{ url, address }` to offer an address to write to as well. It is written as the `List-Unsubscribe` and `List-Unsubscribe-Post` headers; a URL that is not https is refused.
- An address is `'Name <address>'`, a bare address, or `{ name, address }`, which needs no quoting of a name holding a comma.
- Every mail with html goes out with a text part too: the one `text` gives, else one written from the html, links followed by their address, list items dashed, table rows one to a line and a row header written `Label: value`, what the html hides, such as the preheader, left out. `htmlToText(html)` is exported.
- `send(message)` renders and sends now, resolving with `{ messageId, accepted, rejected, response }`. Each mail sent, from `send` or the queue, logs one line naming its subject, the recipients the server took and its answer, so an app logs nothing of its own. A mail the server takes for some recipients and refuses for others is sent all the same, and logged naming those refused: it is not retried, which would send it again to those who have it. A send that fails logs the mail and the reason before it throws. `enqueue(message, { delay })` renders now and queues it, resolving with the job's id; a failed send is retried as kay's queues retry, 5 attempts by default, each wait twice the last from 10 seconds, and a mail given up after its last attempt is logged naming it and the reason, then handed to `queue.onFailed` if given. `render(message)` gives the rendered `Mail` without sending it. `drain()` sends every queued mail due, here and now, for a script.

## Testing

Under `bun test` mails go to the outbox, with no SMTP server to stub:

```ts
import { outbox } from '@kaynooo/kayjs-mail'
import { beforeEach, expect, it } from 'bun:test'
import { testSite } from 'kay/test'
import { signUp } from '../src/routes/index.kay'

const site = await testSite()

beforeEach(() => outbox.clear())

it('welcomes a new account', async () => {
  await site.submit(signUp, { name: 'Ada', email: 'ada@example.com' }, { from: '/' })
  await site.runJobs()

  expect(outbox.to('ada@example.com')[0]?.subject).toBe('Welcome, Ada')
})
```

- `outbox.mails` lists the mails sent, oldest first, each a `Mail` with `id` and `sentAt`; `last()`, `to(address)` (among `to`, `cc` and `bcc`, any case), `find(id)` and `clear()` read it. It keeps the last 500.
- `outbox.links(mail)` gives the addresses a mail links to, in order, each once, as a confirmation test needs: its html's links, or the URLs its text holds. `await outbox.waitFor(address, { timeout })` resolves with the newest mail to that address once one is there, failing after `timeout`, 5 seconds by default, for a mail a server sends on its own time. `outbox.watch(listener)` calls `listener` with each mail sent from then on, until the function it returns is called.
- A browser test driving `kay dev` from another process, as Playwright does, reads the outbox from `/_kay/mail.json`, served in development only: every mail, oldest first, with its html, text and headers, an attachment's bytes in base64 (`encoding: 'base64'`); `?to=<address>` keeps the mails to that address.
- An enqueued mail reaches the outbox once the queue runs: `site.runJobs()` from `kay/test`, or the mailer's `drain()`.

## Development

Under `kay dev`, which sets `NODE_ENV=development`, each mail sent is logged with its subject and kept in the outbox, and `/_kay/mail` lists them, newest first, each with its headers, its size, its html in a sandboxed frame and its text. The list reloads as mails arrive and can be cleared, a mail's html shows at desktop or phone width (`?view=phone`), its size warns past the 102 KB of html Gmail clips at, and it downloads as the `.eml` SMTP would send. The outbox lives in the server's process: a restart empties it.

`/_kay/mail/samples` shows the app's mails without sending any: every `.kay` file under `src/mails`, each rendered as the mailer renders it, html at desktop or phone width and text, with the props its `<name>.preview.ts` beside it default-exports, or none without one; a mail that throws shows why. The page reloads when `kay dev` restarts the server for a changed file.

A mail in the outbox and a sample can each be sent for real from its page, to an address typed in its form, over the SMTP the environment names: `SMTP_HOST`, `SMTP_PORT`, `SMTP_USER` and `SMTP_PASS`, and `SMTP_FROM` unless `mailer({ from })` gives the sender, read on the first send. It goes to that address alone, its `cc` and `bcc` dropped, and nothing else leaves the outbox. `SMTP_HOST` naming a local mailpit puts it there; a real relay puts it in a real inbox, to see what Gmail or Outlook make of it. Without them the page names the variables missing instead of the form, and a post from another site is refused.

```ts
// src/mails/welcome.preview.ts
import type Welcome from './welcome.kay'

export default { name: 'Ada', url: 'https://example.com/confirm' } satisfies Parameters<typeof Welcome>[0]
```

## Other transports

`transport` takes any `{ send(mail) }` resolving with a `Delivery`, such as a provider's HTTP API. `smtp({ host, port, user, pass, name, timeout, maxConnections, rateLimit, dkim: { domain, selector, privateKey } })` is the SMTP one, for settings read some other way. `outbox` is a transport too, for a staging server that must never send.

## kayjs-auth

kayjs-auth's `email.mailer` takes the mailer's `send` or `enqueue`: `email: { mailer: { send: mail.enqueue } }` queues its security mails and retries them.
